title: Exercise Alone Can Tackle Six of the 14 Known Dementia Risk Factors — and South Asians Stand to Gain the Most
excerpt: A University of Minnesota review finds that consistent physical activity can prevent or delay up to half of all dementia cases by managing obesity, hypertension, diabetes, depression, cholesterol and inactivity — the very conditions that disproportionately affect the Indian diaspora.
body:
Nearly half of all dementia cases in Americans over 55 may be preventable — and one intervention addresses more of the known risk factors than any drug, diet or supplement on the market. That intervention is exercise.

A review led by Dereck Salisbury, an associate professor at the University of Minnesota School of Nursing, identifies 14 modifiable lifestyle and environmental factors that shape an individual's risk of cognitive decline. Of those 14, six can be directly managed through a single behaviour: consistent physical activity. Exercise reduces obesity, lowers blood pressure, improves blood-sugar regulation, alleviates depression, brings down cholesterol and, by definition, eliminates physical inactivity.

"Moving your body helps protect brain health by actively mitigating six of the most critical risk factors," Salisbury said, noting that the cascade effect protects vascular health, reduces systemic inflammation and lowers the likelihood of premature cognitive decline.

## The Dose That Matters

A separate study published in *Nature Medicine* adds precision to the prescription. Researchers tracked cognitively unimpaired older adults with pedometer-measured step counts and found that higher physical activity was associated with slower accumulation of tau protein — one of the hallmarks of Alzheimer's pathology — in the brain's inferior temporal region. Crucially, the benefits plateaued at a surprisingly modest level: between 5,000 and 7,500 steps per day.

That finding matters because it reframes the conversation. The goal is not marathon training or crushing a gym PR. A brisk 40-to-50-minute walk most days of the week may be enough to meaningfully slow the biological machinery of Alzheimer's disease.

## Why This Hits Home for South Asians

For the Indian diaspora, these findings carry particular urgency. South Asians are already known to develop cardiovascular disease a decade earlier than other ethnic groups. A scoping review protocol published in *BMJ Open* in 2026 notes that Asian Indian immigrants in the United States experience cardiovascular disease prevalence rates as high as 13 percent among males — significantly higher than other Asian subgroups and the general US population. The underlying drivers are exactly the metabolic conditions that exercise targets: insulin resistance, visceral adiposity, hypertension and dyslipidaemia.

A related study from Knowridge Science Report underscores the connection further. Researchers found that poor metabolic health — measured through routine markers like BMI, blood pressure, cholesterol and glucose — was associated with reduced cerebral blood flow and worse cognitive flexibility, even in young and middle-aged adults. The relationship appeared stronger in women than in men.

The "thin-fat" phenotype common among South Asians, where normal BMI masks high visceral fat and insulin resistance, makes this doubly relevant. Standard screening may declare you healthy while the metabolic damage that accelerates brain ageing is already under way.

## What the Diaspora Can Do

For NRI families, the practical takeaways are clear. First, the exercise threshold is lower than most people assume. Five thousand steps a day — roughly a 40-minute walk — is the floor at which measurable neuroprotective benefits begin. Second, the benefits compound: exercise simultaneously attacks obesity, blood pressure, blood sugar, cholesterol, depression and inactivity, creating a virtuous cycle that no single medication can replicate.

Third, and perhaps most importantly, these findings argue for starting early. The Nature Medicine study specifically examined cognitively unimpaired individuals — people who had not yet shown symptoms. By the time memory complaints surface, tau pathology may already be advanced.

For those with ageing parents in India or in the diaspora, the conversation need not start with a neurology referral. It can start with a pair of walking shoes and a daily 5,000-step goal. The science says that may be enough to change the trajectory.

*Sources: University of Minnesota School of Nursing; Nature Medicine; Knowridge Science Report; BMJ Open*
